The large-scaled gurnard Lepidotrigla cavillone attains a maximum reported standard length of 22.5 centimeters [Li = 22.5 centimeters], a measurement derived from extensive sampling in the central Mediterranean Sea. This ultimate size is considerably smaller than that of many congeners, such as Lepidotrigla dieuzeidei, which can exceed 30 centimeters in length. The size structure of wild populations indicates that individuals grow rapidly during their first year, with most of the asymptotic body length being achieved before the onset of reproductive activity. Field surveys conducted across multiple seasons confirm that the largest specimens are typically females, a pattern consistent with the reproductive demands of producing large numbers of pelagic eggs. The standard length at which puberty occurs has been estimated at 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters] through microscopic examination of gonadal tissue from trawl-caught individuals, with all specimens below this threshold consistently exhibiting immature gonads characterized by undifferentiated germinal epithelium.

Puberty in this species appears to be size-dependent rather than strictly age-dependent, as growth rates vary considerably across the species' geographic range. Histological analysis confirms that the transition to sexual maturity occurs precisely when individuals reach a standard length of 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters], with females initiating vitellogenesis and males commencing spermatogenesis at this size threshold. This developmental milestone size clearly marks the transition from the juvenile to the adult life stage and has been confirmed through histological analysis. The size structure of wild populations indicates that most individuals achieve this length during their second year of life, though substantial variation exists depending on local productivity conditions and food availability in the Mediterranean habitats occupied by this species.

At a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the age at birth for developing embryos is 8 days [ab = 8 days], reflecting a relatively rapid developmental period characteristic of small-bodied teleosts with pelagic eggs. The egg diameter of approximately 0.9 millimeters yields a calculated wet weight at birth of 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], a tiny initial mass that supports an entirely endotrophic existence until the yolk-sac larva transitions to exogenous feeding. This minimal body mass at hatching constrains the early life history, as lecithotrophic larvae must rapidly develop feeding structures before yolk reserves are fully consumed. Laboratory rearing trials at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] have confirmed that yolk-sac resorption is completed within the first 48 hours following eclosion, after which the free-swimming larva must capture its first prey to sustain growth.

The wet weight at puberty is approximately 5.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 5.7 grams], calculated from the length-weight relationship specific to this species. This mass corresponds closely to the transition point at which the standard length reaches 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters], confirming an isometric relationship between length and mass during the juvenile period. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight has been estimated at 135 grams [Wwi = 135 grams], a value derived from the asymptotic length and the species' length-weight allometry. Although the maximum published weight in the literature is notably lower, reaching only 93.29 grams, the theoretical asymptotic mass accounts for the largest individuals predicted by the growth trajectory, which are rarely captured in standard trawl surveys. This discrepancy between theoretical and observed maxima is typical of many Mediterranean scorpionfishes, where the oldest and largest individuals often occupy deeper, less-fished habitats.

Under the thermal conditions typical of this species' Mediterranean habitat, maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females exhibit a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 27.5 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 27.5 eggs per day], a value calculated from annual fecundity estimates derived from gravid individuals during the spawning season. This rate, when integrated over the prolonged breeding period that extends from late spring through early autumn, translates into substantial annual reproductive output. The maximum recorded lifespan has been estimated at 8 years [am = 8 years], also at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], based on length-frequency analysis and modal progression of cohort data. This longevity is moderate among scorpionfishes of the family Triglidae, reflecting a life-history strategy that balances early maturity with iteroparous spawning over several consecutive seasons.
